title: Kings Don't Mean a Thing: the sung dominant chord and Armstrong's obbligato
summary: The whole band sang a big raised-fifth chord and Armstrong riffed between phrases, but Chicago never heard the arrangement.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Yes, that's right. So, that's the way it was. Now, about that 'Kings Don't Mean A Thing.' That's something was beautiful. The way we had that arrangement, and when the band would say, 'Kings Don't Mean A Thing', see, the

whole band would spread with one of those big, blown up chords, like a dominant ninth chord with the fifth raised, and everybody is singing the tones and singing it in tune. And Louis would come through there, (musical sounds). See?
Yeah, singing and there he'd come again.
When you say singing, you mean actually with their voices, or you mean the arrangement --
With their voices. And then Louis would sing --

And then Louis would -- yes, Louis would -- we called it riff. Louis would make a riff, all up and down the -- novelty, nothing but an obbligato passage. That's what it is, yeah, musically speaking, he'd do an obbligato passage in there. But street language, or musicians' language, he riffing all in between there, you know.

And that kept up, 'On The Street Of Dreams,' (musical sounds). Then we'd start. And then Louis would start in -- (musical sounds). And when he said On The Street Of Dreams, he hit that chord, he'd bring it down and the chord would just melt and your tones are melting, and it was pretty.
So, unfortunately, Chicago had never heard it.
